title: Being with the dying
hookLine: a sick monk left alone, a teacher with a basin of water, and a line Christians know too
tomorrow: and when you do have to speak, what do you say?

lines: A SPEECH PRACTICED AT RED LIGHTS.
cards: On the way to a hospital room, people tend to rehearse. Flowers, a balloon, a speech practiced at red lights, something wise to say, or a card that says it better. Then the door opens, and the speech falls apart.
So what do you actually bring into a room where someone is dying? One question for today, and an old answer that's mostly about hands.

teach.b: The Buddhist rule book for monks and nuns tells this story. The Buddha and Ananda, walking through the dwellings, find a monk sick with dysentery, lying in his own mess. Nobody is looking after him.
Why not? I'm no use to the other monks, he says, so they don't tend me. The Buddha doesn't give a talk.
He sends Ananda for water. Together they wash the man and lift him onto a bed. The monk thought he was no use.
The water said otherwise. Only then does the Buddha gather the monks. You have no mother and no father here to tend you, he says.
If you don't tend one another, who will? Whoever would tend me should tend the sick. That's the Buddhist answer: you bring yourself.
Your hands, your time, your staying. Here's something shared.

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
teach.b: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus describes the king at the judgment saying: "I was sick, and ye visited me." And then: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
Two teachers, in two traditions, saying the sick room is where you meet them. And one honest difference. Christians read Matthew as Christ himself present in the one who suffers.
In the rule book, the Buddha doesn't say he is inside the sick monk. He tells monks who left their families that they have to be family to each other now.

how: Buddhist monastics and lay volunteers visit the sick and dying, often sitting quietly, offering care and chanting if wished; many Buddhist hospices and chaplaincies train volunteers in simply being present.

games.q: what does “being with the dying” mean?
o: staying close to someone near death, with care more than words
explaining to a dying person what happens after death
the rules for preparing a body before a funeral

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: said he was no use to the others
washed him and lifted him to a bed
whoever would tend me, tend the sick
I was sick, and ye visited me

s: in the story, the Buddha first gives the sick monk a teaching
water first: he and Ananda wash the man and lift him onto a bed. the talk comes later, to the other monks.
the Buddha told the monks they had no mother or father there to tend them
so they had to tend one another.
the Gospel line and the Buddhist story give the same reason for visiting the sick
Christians read Christ present in the one who suffers; the Buddha tells monks to be each other's family. different reasons, the same care.

games.q: a neighbor you hardly know is very ill, and her family is worn out. you have no wise words. what does today's story suggest?
o: stay away; you don't know her well enough to have anything to offer.
offer a practical hand, a meal, an hour's sitting, and let words come later.
write her a long letter about how to face death calmly.
games.why: the Buddha's first act was water and a bed, not a teaching. bring yourself; the words can wait.

practice: If someone is near you, sit beside them for the whole sit without needing to talk. If you're alone, choose one sound in the room, a fan, a fridge, traffic, and keep it company. Don't analyze it or wait for it to end.
Just stay with it, the way you'd stay with a friend.

wordCard.voice: Being with the dying: bringing yourself, your hands and your time, before any words. Whoever would tend me should tend the sick.

orig.note: Pali gilana: sick, ill. the rule book's section on caring for the sick.

carryVoice: For the road: just be there, the way the water came before the talk. Day nineteen, kept company.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 8.26 (the monk with dysentery; the Buddha and Ananda wash him; 'whoever would tend me should tend the sick')
